newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Accord reached to tone down Cyprus tension - envoy.
newsitem.headline: Accord reached to tone down Cyprus tension - envoy.

text.p: A U.S. envoy on a peace mission to Cyprus said on Monday the two rival sides on the militarily divided island had agreed to United Nations proposals to reduce tension along a ceasefire line separating them.

"Both sides today gave their support to very quick and immediate implementation of that pack of proposals," U.S. State Department official Carey Cavanaugh said before leaving the island for Athens for a further round of talks on Cyprus.

Cavanaugh, dispatched to the island to defuse a row which has broken out after Cyprus's decision to purchase Russian anti-aircraft missiles and Turkish threats of a military strike to stop their deployment, said the proposals would be a boost towards toning down tension between the two sides.
The U.N. force stationed on the island has been holding talks with the military on both sides for several months in an effort to reach agreement on their proposals.

They relate to the unloading of live ammunition among troops on either side of the 180-km (110-mile) ceasefire line which has split Cyprus's Greek and Turkish Cypriot communities for two decades, and unmanning sentry posts. It also imposes a code of conduct for the soldiers to follow.
"These measures reduce the likelihood of incidents along the ceasefire line," Cavanaugh said. "It drops the potential where people worry, people panic unexpectedly and have a gun and fire it.
If the ammunition is in your kit or somewhere else it takes a lot more conscious effort to get to the point where you would use it and hopefully by that time cool-headedness will prevail," he said.
The American official earlier said an imminent crisis in Cyprus had been defused because its government had assured him it would not bring in any part the system for at least 16 months.

Turkey -- which has occupied the northern third of the island since 1974 -- threatened military action several times last week to stop deployment of the S-300 system which the Cypriot government said it would acquire from Russia.
The Turkish Cypriot administration in the north of the island and Turkey have said they will not allow the deployment of the missiles, which the Greek Cypriots say are purely defensive.
"We will do all that is necessary in order to avert the arrival of the missiles," Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash said after meeting Cavanaugh on Monday afternoon.
"After 16 months, if they arrive, they create the crisis again. Turkey has made it absolutely clear that it will not allow the missiles to come," he said.
Cavanaugh, whose government has criticised Cyprus's decision to purchase the system, reiterated that any Turkish response would be unacceptable and unjustified.
He said that any crisis has been "significantly postponed".
"It has moved so far into the future that there should be adequate time to work to address the problem," he said.
The Cypriot government has said it will go ahead with the installation of the system if after 16 months no breakthrough has been made.
Cyprus has been divided since 1974 when Turkey invaded the north of the island after a coup in Nicosia engineered by the military junta then ruling Greece.
Turkey has around 30,000 troops in the north of Cyprus as opposed to 11,500 men of the Greek Cypriot national guard in the south.
